description:
We are team Zizzlelab and we make games and toys that teach young kids invention literacy: how things work, and what it takes to invent something.

Failsafe is our Mars mission game for ages 3 - 12 where kids learn the mindset of failure as data. Most mission games end at game over. Ours asks them to try, crash, fix and try again. Every flop is celebrated and counted, beside NASA's own record of the failures behind it's famous wins. It's a research backed way to change how kids think.
summary:
Kids who see failure as safe try harder things, keep going longer, and bounce back better.This is why we created Failsafe: crash it, fix it, try again, a browser game that teaches children aged 3 to 12 how real engineers work, by letting them build a Mars rover, fail, learn from it and iterate. Like in real life progress in the game stems from things that don't work. Rather than having one right answer our game is open-ended and there are many solutions for the same problem.

The setup: A crew is coming to Mars and needs water, air, a shield and power. Players scout a real NASA image of Mars, build a rover from parts, and drive it across four real rover panoramas by real physics. Wheels tear on sharp rocks, sand traps them, and a dust storm hides the sun. Every part has weight, so no choice is free: a solar panel is light but sleeps in a storm, and nuclear power never sleeps but is very heavy. A flop never ends the game. It is played big, explained, stamped in an Inventor Passport, and sent back to the lab as a clue. After each trip the base faces one real solar flare from NASA's DONKI records, and astronauts land only when it can keep them safe.

This matters because most games treat failure as the end, and NASA treats it as data. The first U.S. win at the Moon came on try 5, and the builders of Curiosity wrote at least 2,865 problem reports. Failsafe shows children those real numbers and lets them live it. Nothing needs reading, so a four-year-old can play too.
